sections.html:
Independence is a fast-growing suburb in the middle of Kenton County, and owners outnumber renters by better than five to one. The owner rate is 83.8% and median household income is $102,361. A seller here is usually a family with equity, a home in good repair and a mortgage to pay off.

Growth explains that profile. The city counted 1,715 people in 1970 and 28,676 in 2020, and the July 2025 estimate is 30,198, a rise of about 5% since 2020. The rest of this page covers permits, taxes and timing.

The typical owner-occupied home is valued at $263,700, and owners with a mortgage report median monthly costs of $1,666. Rent runs $1,250 at the median, and the average household has 3.00 people. Children under 18 are 27.9% of residents, and 10.7% of residents are 65 or older.

Some 92.9% of residents lived in the same house a year earlier. Few households move in a given year, so a house with deferred repairs competes with few other listings that need work, and buyers compare yours against move-in-ready homes. Get itemized repair bids early.

The city borders Elsmere, Erlanger, Covington and Ryland Heights, and its western edge follows the Boone County line near Florence. The original center is in the southeast along Madison Pike. Kentucky Route 17, a four-lane divided road, runs just east of it, 11 miles to downtown Covington. Most of the city drains to Banklick Creek, a Licking River tributary.

Kenton County was formed in 1840, and Independence shares county seat status with Covington. Mean commute is 27.2 minutes. Buyers ask about school zones and parks more than almost anything else. Some parts of the city are zoned for Woodland Middle School and Scott High School instead of Twenhofel Middle School and Simon Kenton High School, so confirm the attendance zone for the address you are selling. Nearby parks include Independence Park, Memorial Park, Pioneer Park and Doe Run Lake. Have both in your listing notes.

sections.h2: Permits and inspections before a sale
sections.html:
No permit is needed just to sell, but unfinished or unpermitted work can stall a closing. The city runs an online permit portal for joint building and zoning applications, covering new homes, additions, decks, sheds and basement finishes. Confirm that every past project on your house has a closed permit. Applications ask for these uploads.

Uploads the Independence permit portal asks for
UploadDetail
Affidavit of AssurancesSigned and notarized for any permit with a building-code review; not required for fences, above-ground pools or small sheds
Site planRequired with the application
Building plansRequired with the application
Contractor occupational licenseFor contractors named on the application, through the county occupational office
Contractor liability insuranceFor contractors named on the application

Electrical and plumbing permits go through separate inspector offices, which the portal page lists. Heating and cooling permits are issued to master HVAC contractors except where a homeowner permit applies. A notary at the city building is available on weekdays from 8:00 to 4:30, and inspections are scheduled by text message to the number on the portal page. Planning and Development Services of Kenton County administers zoning and publishes the Independence zoning ordinance online.

The Kenton County Sheriff collects current real estate bills through April 15 each year. After April 16, bills move to the County Clerk's real estate department. The Clerk keeps an Independence office at 5272 Madison Pike, open weekdays from 7:30 to 4:00, so you can record a deed or ask about a payoff without driving to Covington.

The Clerk will not prepare documents or supply blank forms, so a title company or attorney drafts the deed. The deed tax under KRS 142.050 is 50 cents per $500, rounded up, charged to the grantor and collected before recording.

For questions on assessment or a homestead or disability exemption, contact the Kenton County Property Valuation Administrator. January 1 is the assessment date, and the roll is open for inspection for 13 days starting the first Monday in May. An appeal at the county clerk's office comes only after a conference with the PVA.

Title work goes faster with a ready folder. Pull these together before you say yes to anyone:

  • The deed and a legal description that matches the Kenton County records, which are searchable online through the clerk.
  • The most recent tax bill and the name of the office that collected it, the Sheriff before April 16 or the Clerk after.
  • Permit numbers for additions, decks, finished basements and sheds, plus closed inspection records.
  • A lender payoff letter and the name of any contractor who may have filed a claim.

Have your closing agent compare the parcel details on the deed against the PVA's records.

Once you have a signed contract, the title company or attorney searches the Kenton County records, drafts the deed and orders payoffs. The mortgage is paid from your proceeds, and the tax bill is credited between you and the buyer for the months each of you owns the house. Ask whether the sheriff or the clerk holds the bill, since the answer changes with the calendar.

At the signing you sign the deed, the deed tax is paid, and the deed is recorded at the clerk's office. If a contractor ever filed a claim against the house, it has to be cleared first. Afterward, confirm the mortgage release was posted so the old loan no longer shows against the property. Keep a copy of the recorded deed and the settlement statement for your tax records, and file a change of address so later notices from the county reach you.

Start with what you control: permit history, lender payoff letter, latest tax bill. Then choose a route.

  • List with an agent and price near recent neighborhood sales. Strong fit when the house is clean and updated.
  • Sell as-is for cash. Fits a job transfer, an estate or a house that needs a roof or a kitchen.
  • Repair first. Worth it only if the work costs less than the price gap it closes.

With a median value above $260,000, even a modest repair bill runs to five figures, so request itemized bids before choosing. A cash sale avoids the appraisal and lender timeline, and you set the closing date with the buyer.

faqs.q: Do Independence homes sell faster than the Kentucky average?
faqs.a: The owner market is tight, with a 2.7% vacancy rate in 2020 and only 0.7% homeowner vacancy, so well-priced houses draw interest quickly. Speed still depends on price, condition and how the buyer pays.

faqs.q: Who collects property tax on an Independence house?
faqs.a: The Kenton County Sheriff collects the current bill through April 15. After April 16 the bill is delinquent and the Kenton County Clerk's real estate department handles it. Pay or credit any open amount at closing.

faqs.q: What is the Kentucky deed tax on an Independence sale?
faqs.a: The seller pays 50 cents for each $500 of value, rounded up, under KRS 142.050, collected by the clerk at recording. Foreclosure transfers are exempt.

faqs.q: Do I need a permit to sell an Independence house with a finished basement?
faqs.a: Selling needs no permit, but a finished basement or deck built without one can cause questions at inspection or closing. The city's online portal lets you search permits by number or parcel, so check the history before listing.

faqs.q: Where do I record a deed for an Independence property?
faqs.a: At the Kenton County Clerk, which has an office at 5272 Madison Pike in Independence as well as one in Covington. Call the real estate and recording department at 859-392-1650 with questions.
